pedagogy.summary: Mentally adding or subtracting hundreds to a three-digit number is the simplest of the three: within 1000 only the hundreds digit changes, and the tens and ones stay fixed. Children reuse a single-digit fact (3+2 hundreds) at the scale of hundreds. It is the cleanest demonstration of place-value invariance — the local part left untouched — and is taught with a place-value chart and hundred-scaled number line. (Bridging a thousand is a later topic, so within-1000 cases do not bridge.)
bestPractices: Anchor the tens and ones; operate only on the hundreds — 345+200 keeps '_45' and works 3+2 hundreds
Reuse the known single-digit fact at the scale of hundreds (3 hundreds + 2 hundreds = 5 hundreds)
Use a place-value chart to show only the hundreds row changing
Contrast with the ones/tens topics so the child generalises 'the added amount changes its own column'
Ask the child to state which digits stay the same and why (DfE evidence)
keyRepresentations: Place-value / Gattegno chart (only the hundreds row moves)
Place-value counters on a H-T-O grid
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (adding the hundreds amount to the tens or ones)
Miscounting the hundreds (762 − 400 given as 462 vs correct 362 — a single-digit subtraction slip at the hundreds scale)
Disturbing the tens/ones when they should be untouched
Overreaching to bridge a thousand when the numbers don't require it

learn.summary: Year 3 learners mentally add and subtract hundreds to/from a three-digit number with answers below 1000, where only the hundreds digit changes and the tens and ones stay fixed. The core insight is place-value invariance: a known single-digit fact (3+2 hundreds) is reused at the scale of hundreds while the other columns are left untouched. Work with a place-value chart, a number line marked in hundreds, base-ten hundred-flats, partitioning jottings (345 = 300 + 45), and place-value counters on an H-T-O grid; contrast with +tens/+ones (using examples that need no regrouping) so children generalise that an added amount lands in its own column when that column does not go past 9. With answers below 1000 these cases never bridge a thousand.

activities.title: Freeze the tens and ones: only the hundreds move
feedback: If the learner alters the 45 in 345+200, re-anchor on the chart: 200 is two hundreds, so it joins the hundreds. Cover or grey out the tens and ones to show they cannot change, then re-read 545.
If the learner disturbs the tens/ones in subtraction, physically hold or cover the '62' of 762 and only operate on the hundreds.

If the answer to 762−400 comes out as 462, this is most likely a single-digit fact slip (the learner found 4 hundreds instead of 7−4=3 hundreds): rehearse 7−4 on its own, then reapply at the hundreds scale to get 362. The tens and ones were kept, so place value does not need reteaching.
Prompt: 'Is 762−400 bigger or smaller than 762? Should it be?' to catch direction-of-operation errors.
activities.rationale: The objective is place-value invariance, so the activity makes the stable columns visible and asks the learner to predict and name what stays fixed before checking. A manipulable or clearly staged chart lets the learner act on the hundreds while the tens and ones remain visibly still; a static reveal can show the same contrast but does not let the learner operate the pieces.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils add and subtract mentally a three-digit number and hundreds.
Place-value understanding lets a known single-digit fact be reused at the scale of hundreds, with the other columns left invariant (unitising).
learnerActions: Show 345 on a place-value chart (hundreds, tens, ones). Add 200 and watch only the hundreds change from 3 to 5, giving 545 — say aloud that the '45' tail is unchanged.
Now do 762 − 400 on the same chart: the hundreds drop from 7 to 3 while the '62' stays put, giving 362.
Before revealing each answer, point to the tens and ones and state that they will not change, then check after.
Repeat with 518 + 300, predicting the answer (818) and naming which digits stay the same.
Articulate the rule in your own words: the amount you add or take away is a number of hundreds, so it lands only in the hundreds column.
activities.intendedInsight: When the answer stays below 1000, adding or subtracting hundreds changes only the hundreds digit; the tens and ones are invariant because the added amount belongs to the hundreds column.

activities.title: Same place-value idea, one column along
feedback: If the learner moves the change to the wrong column, restate where each amount belongs (200 = hundreds, 20 = tens) and re-anchor on the chart.

If the learner thinks a different column should change when switching between +hundreds and +tens, clarify that adding tens and adding hundreds are simply different amounts, each landing in its own column — there is no rule reversing, just a different column changing.
activities.rationale: Contrasting +hundreds with +tens/+ones helps the learner generalise beyond a single case and prevents the 'change any digit' error. Juxtaposition makes the invariance principle explicit across columns.
sourceClaims: Place-value understanding lets a known single-digit fact be reused at the scale of hundreds, with the other columns left invariant (unitising).
learnerActions: Place a +hundreds example (345 + 200) beside a +tens example (345 + 20) and work both.
For each, say which single column changes and read off the two different answers (545 vs 365).
State the shared principle: when the column does not go past 9 (no regrouping), the added amount changes only its own column and leaves the others alone.
Try a mixed set, e.g. 345+200, 345+20, 345+2, naming the changing digit each time before answering.
activities.intendedInsight: The place-value rule generalises: whether you add hundreds, tens, or ones, the added amount changes only its own column as long as that column does not go past 9 (no regrouping), as in 345+200, 345+20 and 345+2.

activities.title: Explain what stays the same
feedback: Full understanding: answers quickly in the head, keeps tens and ones untouched, and explains that only the hundreds change because the added amount is a number of hundreds.

Partial: reaches answers with the chart or number line but is unsure which digits stay fixed, or makes single-digit hundreds slips — revisit the invariance naming step and rehearse the hundreds facts.
Gap: changes the tens/ones or lands the hundreds in the wrong column and cannot say what stays the same — return to the chart activity with the tens and ones covered.
activities.rationale: Articulating which digits stay fixed surfaces whether the learner understands invariance or is guessing, and separates a conceptual gap from a mere single-digit fact slip. Reasoning-focused discussion complements, rather than replaces, the hands-on chart work.
learnerActions: After each, answer: which digits changed and which stayed exactly the same, and why?
Answer the probes: How is 762−400 like 7−4, and what is different? If it were 345+20 instead of 345+200, which digit would change?
Explain in a sentence why the tens and ones do not change.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to state that only the hundreds digit changes — and why — demonstrates genuine place-value understanding rather than a memorised procedure.

activities.title: Quick checks for the two common slips
feedback: A 462 answer signals a 7−4 fact slip at the hundreds scale: rehearse the single-digit fact and reapply to reach 362.
An answer where the tens/ones changed signals a wrong-column error: re-anchor on the chart and name the column the added amount belongs to.
activities.rationale: Rapid, mixed items are efficient for rehearsal and for catching the two predicted error patterns, and asking for a brief justification adds a little reasoning; even so, they do not by themselves demand the sustained construction and explanation of the chart activities, so they follow rather than replace them.
learnerActions: Answer rapid items such as 762 − 400, choosing between 362 and a tempting 462, and justify the correct choice.
Work items that mix +hundreds with +tens (e.g. 345+200 next to 345+20) and state which column moved before answering.
For any item where the tens or ones changed, go back and re-anchor on the chart.
activities.intendedInsight: Fast, mixed practice rehearses the skill and exposes wrong-digit and single-digit miscount slips.

constraints: Keep all answers below 1000 so they never bridge a thousand; bridging a thousand is a later topic and should not be introduced here.

Recognition/multiple-choice items check fluency and catch slips but do not by themselves require the learner to construct or sustain the reasoning — use them after, not instead of, the chart and explanation activities.
A static reveal can show which digit changes but does not let the learner operate the pieces; prefer a manipulable chart when the goal is for the learner to act on the hundreds.
Distinguish a single-digit hundreds-fact slip (762−400→462) from a place-value gap: the first is a fact rehearsal, not a reason to reteach place value.
Base-ten hundred-flats and place-value counters are physical approximations of the abstract place-value structure; use them as representations, not as the concept itself.
The 462 answer is an error to be diagnosed (correct is 362); never present it as a valid option.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Checked arithmetic: 345+200=545, 762−400=362, 518+300=818, 345+20=365 — all correct. The 462 answer is explicitly an error pattern (should be 362) and is only used as a labelled distractor/slip to diagnose, never presented as valid.
The '3→5' phrasing for the hundreds in 345+200 corresponds to 3 hundreds + 2 hundreds = 5 hundreds, which is correct.

An irrelevant fraction 'denominator flips' framing that had been inserted into the +hundreds vs +tens activity has been kept out; this topic has no denominators and that framing would confuse learners.

Partitioning jottings (345 = 300 + 45) and place-value counters were restored to the summary so the full set of original representations is represented; they can be used interchangeably with the chart.

Non-preferred alternatives (static reveal, spoken reasoning discussion, rapid recognition items) were retained as distinct activities with their stated pedagogical purposes rather than collapsed into the preferred chart approach.

Activities 3 and 4 have sourceClaims set to [] because no original source claim directly supports their specific pedagogical principles (articulation surfacing understanding; rapid items catching slips) beyond the general topic.

probeDeeper: For 345 + 200, which digits stayed exactly the same? Why don't they change?
If it were 345 + 20 instead of 345 + 200, which digit would change then?
Is your answer to 762 − 400 bigger or smaller than 762? Should it be?
assess.correctAnswer: 545, 362, 818. In each, only the hundreds digit changes: 3+2=5 hundreds (545); 7−4=3 hundreds (362); 5+3=8 hundreds (818). The tens and ones stay fixed throughout.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the wrong digit — adds the hundreds amount to the tens or ones ('345 + 200' altering the 45)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor with the chart: 200 is two hundreds, joining the hundreds; grey out the 45 to show it cannot change.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tens or ones change; the hundreds addition lands in the wrong column

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the hundreds — '762 − 400 is 462' (a single-digit subtraction slip at the hundreds scale)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach place value: rehearse the single-digit hundreds fact (7−4=3) then reapply. This is a fact slip, not a place-value gap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tens and ones are correct but the hundreds digit is off by one; underlying 7−4 done as 7−3 or similar

responseLevels.gap: Changes the tens/ones, or lands the hundreds in the wrong column; cannot say what stays the same.
responseLevels.full: Answers all three instantly in his head, keeps the tens and ones untouched, and explains that only the hundreds digit changes because the added amount is a number of hundreds.
responseLevels.partial: Gets answers with the chart or number line but is unsure which digits stay fixed, or makes single-digit hundreds slips.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to do these mentally, thinking aloud: 345 + 200, then 762 − 400, then 518 + 300. After each, ask which digits changed and which stayed the same.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because within 1000 these never bridge a thousand, a fluent child answers almost instantly and can state that the tens and ones are untouched. A child without place-value invariance changes the wrong digit or disturbs the tens/ones; a single-digit slip at the hundreds scale (762−400→462) reveals shaky hundreds facts.
